name: newline-tools
short_description: CLI and Python library for efficient processing of massive text files with operations like shuffling, deduplication, splitting, and sampling.
long_description: Newline Tools is a command-line utility and Python library designed for working with massive text datasets. It provides four main operations: shuffle (randomize line order using buffer-based algorithm), dedupe (remove duplicate lines using Bloom filters), split (divide files by count, size, or proportions), and sample (extract random subsets using reservoir or index sampling). All operations are optimized for memory efficiency with configurable buffer sizes and support progress tracking. The library handles files that are too large to fit in memory by using temporary files and streaming processing.

modules.description: Implements the Shuffle class for randomizing line order in large files using a buffer-based algorithm with multiple shuffling rounds.
Implements the Dedupe class for removing duplicate lines from files using Bloom filters for memory-efficient duplicate detection.
Implements the Split class for dividing files into multiple parts by number of parts, total size, or proportional ratios.
Implements the Sample class for extracting random subsets of lines using reservoir sampling or index-based sampling methods.
Utility functions including count_lines() for efficiently counting total lines in a file.
Package initialization exposing Shuffle, Dedupe, Split, and Sample classes with version metadata.
CLI entry point providing argument parsing and command dispatch for shuffle, dedupe, split, and sample subcommands.
Unit tests for the Shuffle class including tests for randomization quality, edge cases, and statistical distribution.
Unit tests for the Dedupe class covering duplicate removal, empty files, and various duplicate scenarios.
Unit tests for the Split class testing splitting by parts, size, and proportions with various file configurations.
Unit tests for the Sample class covering both reservoir and index sampling methods with edge cases.
